slides.sub: One course outcome, four chapter objectives

items.head: LO-1
items.body: Explain what Bitcoin is, as money and as a system: its history, its units and supply schedule, the parts it is built from - keys, addresses, transactions, blocks, nodes, mining - and the problems it was designed to solve.

Compute Bitcoin's supply schedule and explain why the total stays just below 21 million
Compare wallet types by platform, node type and key control, and choose one for a stated use
Relate the chapter's principle of key-holder control to W3C Decentralized Identifiers

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What is the unit of Bitcoin's currency, how far can it be divided, how much of it will ever exist, and which rule produces that total?
Who creates new bitcoin, on what schedule, and in what sense does the arrangement replace the functions of a central bank?
Which problem of earlier digital money does Bitcoin solve, and which of its four parts answers which part of that problem?
How can a wallet be classified by platform, by autonomy and by the control of keys, and what does each choice cost its user?
What happens, step by step and object by object, between the moment Joe presses Send and the moment Alice's payment is confirmed?

slides.notes: These are the competency questions the chapter's ontology was written to answer, so they are a fair statement of what a student should be able to answer at the end. Come back to them in the recap. A student who can answer all of them has the chapter; a student who can answer none of them has memorised vocabulary.

slides.title: Money
slides.sub: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the…
slides.notes:
A currency is only as useful as the rules that govern it. People accept money because they expect to be able to spend it later at a value they can foresee, and the expectation depends on knowing who can create more of it and how fast. Conventional currencies answer these questions with institutions, namely a central bank and a clearing system, whereas Bitcoin answers them with rules written into software that every participant can read. Understanding the monetary side first makes the technical machinery of the later branches easier to follow, because every mechanism exists to protect one of these monetary rules.

Three misconceptions are worth removing early. First, there is no company or authority that issues bitcoin; the rules of issuance are enforced by every participant. Second, the number of bitcoin is not unlimited, but the limit is a property of the software rules and not a law of nature, so it is only as strong as the agreement of the participants to keep it. Third, a figure such as the price or the current subsidy is a value at a date; the chapter's rules stay fixed while those values change.

slides.title: Unit

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted. It contains the name of the currency, with its distinction between the unit and the system, and the smallest subdivision that can be recorded, the satoshi. Together these give a student the exact vocabulary in which amounts are written in the rest of the course (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The two concepts of this section move from the name to the arithmetic.

slides.notes:
An imprecise vocabulary produces imprecise reasoning. A student who writes that Bitcoin was sent when bitcoin was meant has confused the payment system with the thing that it transports, and an engineer who forgets how amounts are divided will make rounding errors in software that handles real value. The unit section therefore comes first so that every later figure can be stated without ambiguity.

Concepts in this section: Bitcoin Unit, Satoshi (unit).

slides.title: Bitcoin Unit and Satoshi (unit)

items.head: Bitcoin Unit
items.body: Bitcoin is the name of the system, and bitcoin is the name of the unit of currency that the system transports. The book states the convention in a short note: the unit of currency is called bitcoin with a small b, and the system is called Bitcoin with a capital B (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The unit is divisible. The chapter notes that some wallets show an amount in a different denomination, because 0.001 BTC is 1 millibitcoin (mBTC) or 100,000 satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Satoshi (unit)
items.body: A satoshi is the smallest denomination of bitcoin that can be recorded on the blockchain.
The conversion is a multiplication by 10 to the power 8.

slides.notes:
The distinction is more than a matter of spelling. The system consists of a protocol, a network, and software, while the unit is a quantity of value that is recorded by that system. Chapter 1 describes the unit as a currency that is entirely virtual, since there are no physical coins and not even individual digital coins, and it describes the system as a collection of concepts and technologies (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Keeping the two words apart prevents sentences such as a Bitcoin was sent, which blur the difference between the thing that moves and the machinery that moves it.

A common slip is to treat bitcoin as a physical or digital object that can be held in the way that a coin can. The chapter is explicit that coins are implied in transactions that transfer value from spender to receiver, and that no coin object exists (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second slip is to write bitcoin with a capital letter in the middle of a sentence when the unit is meant. The convention is a convention of this textbook; other writers do not always follow it, so a student should read an unfamiliar text with the possibility of a different usage in mind.

---

A currency that is divided into very small pieces can be used for very small payments, and a system that counts in whole units avoids a class of errors. Software represents an amount as an integer number of satoshis, because integers add and subtract exactly, whereas decimal fractions held in floating-point numbers do not always do so. Bitcoin Core, the reference implementation, defines one bitcoin as 100,000,000 of its smallest units and uses a whole-number amount type for the value of every output (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two warnings apply. First, the satoshi must not be confused with Satoshi Nakamoto, although the unit is named after the author. Second, a conversion done with ordinary floating-point numbers can be off by a tiny amount, which is harmless in a classroom exercise and dangerous in software that moves value; the safe habit is to convert at the edges of a program and to compute with whole numbers of satoshis in between.

slides.title: Supply

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This section explains the three ideas behind that sentence: the cap on the total, the halving of the subsidy at fixed intervals, and the subsidy itself, which is the amount of new bitcoin paid to the miner of each block.
The three concepts build on one another. The block subsidy is the quantity that is paid for each block. The halving is the rule that cuts the subsidy in half every 210,000 blocks.

slides.notes:
Predictability is the economic point of the schedule. Anyone can compute in advance how many bitcoin will exist at any future block, and nobody can change the schedule without the agreement of the participants who run the software. For a student, the supply schedule is also the best first example of how a rule of an economic system can be written as a short program and checked by execution.

Concepts in this section: Supply cap, Halving, Block subsidy.

slides.title: Supply cap
slides.sub: the sum of every block subsidy

items.head: What it is
items.body: The supply cap is the upper limit on the total amount of bitcoin that can ever exist. The chapter states it as a fixed total just below 21 million coins, and explains that the number in circulation follows an easily predictable curve in which half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
items.body: The subsidy begins at 50 bitcoin per block.

slides.notes:
A limit on supply is what distinguishes Bitcoin from a currency that a central bank can expand. Because the rule is enforced by every full node, a miner who tries to claim more than the rule allows produces a block that the other participants reject. The chapter adds that nobody can force you to accept any bitcoins that were created beyond the expected issuance rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cap therefore is a promise about future behaviour that is backed by the participants' own software and not by the word of an issuer.

A cap is a rule of the software and not a physical law. It holds as long as the participants who run full nodes continue to enforce it, and changing it would require nearly all of them to agree on new software, which is why the schedule is regarded as stable. A second caution concerns the phrase just below 21 million: the true total is 20999999.9769 bitcoin, so a program that assumes exactly 21,000,000 will be off by a small but real amount. A third caution is that the cap says nothing about coins whose keys are lost; those remain counted in the supply although no one can spend them.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Halving

items.head: What it is
items.body: A halving is the event at which the block subsidy is cut in half. The rule is part of the protocol: the chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, and that half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The program divides the block height by 210000 to find the number of halvings that have already happened, and it shifts the initial subsidy of 50 * 10**8 satoshis to the right by that many places.

slides.notes:
The halving is the mechanism that makes the supply curve geometric. Each interval pays half as much as the one before, so the total converges to a limit instead of growing without end, and the issuance of new bitcoin becomes less and less important compared with the fees paid by transactions. The halving also changes the economics of mining at fixed dates, because a miner's revenue from new bitcoin drops by half on that day.

The chapter says that a halving happens about every four years, and the text of the course must not state this as an exact calendar fact. The interval is a number of blocks, 210000, and the calendar time depends on how fast blocks are actually found; at the target of one block every 10 minutes it comes to a little less than four years (210000 blocks of 10 minutes each last 3.99 years). The dates of later halvings are therefore estimates until they occur.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block subsidy

items.head: What it is
items.body: The block subsidy is the amount of newly created bitcoin that the rules allow the miner of a block to claim. The chapter describes the payment in general terms: on average every 10 minutes one miner can add security to past transactions, and is rewarded with both brand new bitcoins and the fees paid by recent transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
items.body: The subsidy depends only on the block height.

slides.notes:
The subsidy is the only way in which new bitcoin enters circulation, so it is at once the supply policy and the payment for the work of securing the network. The whitepaper explains the design: the first transaction in a block is a special transaction that starts a new coin owned by the creator of the block, which adds an incentive for nodes to support the network and provides a way to distribute coins into circulation in the absence of a central authority (Nakamoto, 2008). The same paper compares the steady addition of coins with gold miners who expend resources to add gold to circulation.

The subsidy is not the same as the reward: the reward of a block is the subsidy plus the fees of its transactions, and the glossary of the book describes the reward as the amount included in each new block for the miner who found the proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The figure in that glossary entry, 12.5 bitcoin, was the subsidy at the time the glossary was written and is out of date. Because the subsidy keeps halving, the fees become a larger share of the reward over time, a development the whitepaper anticipated when it says that the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees (Nakamoto, 2008).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Price

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin. The chapter's short answer is that the price is set by markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The section contains the idea of a floating exchange rate and the way in which a single quotation is computed from the many trades that happen in different places.
The first concept in the section explains why the rate floats and how it is quoted as a currency pair.

slides.notes:
Bitcoin has no issuer who could announce a price, and it has no central bank that could fix an exchange rate against another currency. The price therefore has to be discovered, and the quality of the discovery determines whether two people can agree on how much cash is worth a given amount of bitcoin, as Alice and Joe must before their exchange.

Concepts in this section: Floating exchange rate, Volume-weighted average.

slides.title: Floating exchange rate

items.head: What it is
items.body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and a floating exchange rate is one that is not fixed by any authority but moves according to the demand for the currencies and the amount available.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The conversion itself is a multiplication. If the rate were 60,000 dollars per bitcoin, the amount of 0.001 bitcoin that Alice buys would be worth 0.001 * 60000, which evaluates to 60.0 dollars.

slides.notes:
The explanation answers the question of who sets the price: markets do. This matters for anyone who accepts bitcoin as payment, because the value of the amount received can change between the moment of the agreement and the moment the money is spent. It also explains why the chapter treats the price as an input that Alice and Joe must look up before every exchange, and not as a property of the network itself.

A floating rate is not an error or a defect; it is the ordinary condition of most currencies, and the chapter says so. The risk is the volatility that comes with it, so a merchant who prices goods in a national currency but accepts bitcoin must convert at the moment of sale. A further caution concerns the data: the price shown by one website is the price of one market or one average, and two services may differ slightly, which the next concept explains.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Volume-weighted average
slides.sub: two trades, 3 units at 100 and 1 unit at 104

items.head: What it is
items.body: A volume-weighted average is an average of prices in which each price counts in proportion to the volume traded at that price. The chapter says that a pricing service will aggregate the prices from several markets and calculate a volume-weighted average representing the broad market exchange rate of a currency pair, for example BTC/USD (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The computation multiplies each price by its volume, adds the products, and divides by the total volume.

slides.notes:
A simple average treats a trade of one small unit and a trade of a thousand units as equal, so a single small and unusual trade could move the result. Weighting by volume makes the figure reflect where most of the money actually changed hands. The result is a more stable and more representative reference rate, which is why pricing services and institutional reference rates use this kind of average (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The average is a summary and not a market price that anybody can necessarily trade at. Its value depends on which markets a service includes and on the period over which the trades are collected, so two services can report different numbers for the same currency pair. A volume-weighted average can also lag a fast-moving market, because older trades remain in the window; a person who needs to buy at a specific moment must look at the actual offers on the market where the purchase takes place.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Issuance

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Issuance section is about who creates money and by what rule. In a conventional economy a central bank controls the creation of money, and a clearing system settles payments between banks. The chapter argues that Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank, and it describes the currency as deflationary over the long term (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The four concepts of the section pair the old with the new. The central bank and the clearing house are the institutions that the chapter says Bitcoin replaces.

slides.notes:
Issuance is the point at which Bitcoin differs most from the money that students already know. A central bank can respond to an emergency by creating more money, and a clearing house can reverse or delay a payment, but a rule-based system gives up both powers in exchange for predictability and for independence from any single institution. The section helps a student to judge that trade-off with the institutions in front of him.

Concepts in this section: Central bank, Clearing house, Central bank replacement, Deflation.

slides.title: Central bank and Clearing house

items.head: Central bank
items.body: A central bank is an institution that issues a country's currency and controls how much of it is created. The Bitcoin Wiki describes the arrangement in a centralized economy: currency is issued by a central bank at a rate that is supposed to match the growth of the amount of goods that are exchanged, so that these goods can be traded with stable prices, and the monetary base is controlled by that bank (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
The central bank works by discretion, whereas Bitcoin works by rule.

items.head: Clearing house
items.body: A clearing house is a central institution through which payments are recorded and settled. The chapter describes the role when it discusses the digital money that existed before Bitcoin: early digital currencies used a central clearinghouse to settle all transactions at regular intervals, just like a traditional banking system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The clearing house keeps one authoritative list of who owns what and processes payments against it. Because it sees all payments in order, it can reject a payment that spends money which is already spent.

slides.notes:
The concept is needed in this chapter because the chapter defines Bitcoin partly by contrast. It says that Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student who does not know what a central bank does cannot judge the claim, so the function has to be named: creation of money by an authority, according to a policy that the authority can change.

To say that Bitcoin replaces the central bank is a claim about the function of issuing money, and the chapter does not claim that Bitcoin provides every other service of the institutions it names. The difference between a policy that people can change and a rule that the software enforces is the point of the comparison, and whether the rule is better is a question of economics that this textbook leaves open. The course asks the student to state the difference accurately and to avoid slogans.

---

The clearing house solves a real problem. Someone has to decide which of two conflicting payments counts, and a central party with a global view of the money in circulation can decide it. The same page of the chapter says that conventional money is also often stored and transmitted digitally and that the counterfeiting and double-spend issues are handled by clearing all electronic transactions through central authorities that have a global view of the currency in circulation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cost of the solution is that the whole system depends on one operator.

Removing the clearing house does not remove the need for clearing; it moves the function into the network. The chapter makes this point when it says that mining decentralizes the clearing function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the clearing in Bitcoin is not instantaneous: the chapter says that a transaction is confirmed when it is included in a block, which happens every 10 minutes on average, and until then it is shown as unconfirmed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Central bank replacement

items.head: What it is
items.body: The replacement of the central bank is the chapter's claim about what mining achieves for the system as a whole. In the words of the chapter, Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Two functions are named: issuing the currency and clearing transactions, and mining performs both at once.

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The idea is the thread that connects the early sections of the chapter, where mining is introduced, with the later ones on confirmations and clearing.

slides.notes:
The claim explains why Bitcoin needs mining at all. A network of equal participants has no leader who could decide which transactions come first or who could issue new money, so the work of the miner is the substitute for that leader. The reward of a block creates the currency, and the inclusion of transactions in blocks clears them. The incentive for the miner, new bitcoins and fees, pays for the work that keeps the record secure, as the whitepaper explains (Nakamoto, 2008).

The word replace should be read narrowly. The mechanism replaces the need for a central issuer and a central clearing operator, which are the two functions that the chapter names. It does not make the system free of intermediaries in practice, because the chapter itself describes users who hold their funds with custodians, exchanges and web services, and these are ordinary companies with the usual risks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Deflation
slides.sub: the date when the subsidy reaches zero

items.head: What it is
items.body: Deflation is an increase in the real value of the monetary unit, reflected in a decrease in the general price level of goods and services (Wikipedia contributors, 2026).

items.head: How it works
items.body: The first block of the network was created on 2009-01-03 at 18:15:05 UTC, according to the time stamp 1231006505 in the block data (Blockstream, 2026).

slides.notes:
The concept matters because it is one of the first things that economists say about Bitcoin, and it follows directly from the rules of the previous section. If the money supply grows by a shrinking amount while demand for the money does not shrink, each unit tends to buy more over time. The chapter adds a related remark, that nobody can force you to accept any bitcoins that were created beyond the expected issuance rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Both statements come from the same schedule.

Deflationary does not mean that the price of bitcoin must rise, and the chapter does not say so; it describes the issuance. The effect on prices is a question of economics that depends on many factors besides the supply schedule. Finally, the end of the subsidy does not end mining: the miner's income then consists of fees, which is why the whitepaper observes that the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees and be completely inflation free (Nakamoto, 2008).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Network
slides.sub: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader.
slides.notes:
A money system that is held together by many independent computers must solve a hard problem: those computers have to agree on which payments happened, even though they receive messages in different orders and some of them may be dishonest. The solution is the main technical achievement of Bitcoin, and the chapter presents it as a breakthrough in distributed computing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Without an understanding of the agreement mechanism, the rest of the course reads as a list of unrelated parts.

It is easy to imagine the network as a company with servers, and the chapter warns against that picture; there is no central server. It is equally easy to imagine consensus as a vote of people, whereas the agreement is reached by software that checks the same rules and follows the chain with the most work. The branch should be read with both corrections in mind.

slides.title: Consensus

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions. The chapter says that the proof-of-work algorithm is a mechanism for reaching global decentralized consensus on the valid blockchain, and that a key innovation was to use a distributed computation system to conduct a global lottery every 10 minutes on average, allowing the decentralized network to arrive at consensus about the state of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The section contains five concepts. Proof of work is the costly computation that makes a block hard to produce and easy to check.

slides.notes:
Consensus is what turns a crowd of computers into a ledger. Without it, two participants could hold different histories and each could claim that the other's payments never happened. The consensus mechanism is also what protects against the double-spend, the main threat to any digital money, so the concepts of this section explain the security of the entire system.

Concepts in this section: Proof of work, Double-spend, Mining, Difficulty adjustment, Byzantine Generals' Problem.

slides.title: Proof of work
slides.sub: a toy search for a hash starting with 0000

items.head: What it is
items.body: Proof of work is a way of showing that a certain amount of computation has been spent, in a form that anyone can check cheaply. In Bitcoin it is the method by which the network decides which block comes next.

rows: next(n for n in range(10**6) if hashlib.sha256(f'SEN0401-{n}'.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000'))

items.head: How it works
items.body: The example is a miniature of the real process.

slides.notes:
The purpose of the work is to make agreement possible without trust. If producing a block were free, anyone could produce as many as they liked and the network could not choose between them. By making each block costly, proof of work turns the choice into a measurable quantity: the whitepaper observes that proof of work is essentially one-CPU-one-vote, and that the majority decision is represented by the longest chain, the one with the greatest proof-of-work effort invested in it (Nakamoto, 2008). This also solves the problem that a vote by network address could be subverted by anyone able to allocate many addresses.

Proof of work does not prove that the transactions in a block are valid; validity is checked separately by every node, and a block with an invalid transaction is rejected however much work was spent on it. The work is also not useful computation in itself: its value lies in its cost. A further misconception is that the work is a puzzle that can be solved by cleverness; since a hash function behaves unpredictably, the only method is to try values, and the winner is determined by chance in proportion to the computing power used.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Double-spend

items.head: What it is
items.body: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

rows: [(c not in s) and not s.add(c) for s in [set()] for c in ('coin7', 'coin7')]

items.head: How it works
items.body: The defence is a public, ordered record.

slides.notes:
A digital currency that cannot prevent double-spending is worthless, since the recipient could never be sure that the money received had not already been paid to someone else. Before Bitcoin the problem was handled by clearing every transaction through a central clearinghouse; the chapter calls this a weakness because the central party becomes a single point of attack, and it says that Nakamoto's proof of work elegantly solves the problem without it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A double-spend is not made impossible by cryptography alone; a digital signature proves who authorised a payment and does not show that the payment is the only one. The protection is a consequence of consensus and gets stronger with each confirmation, so a transaction that is not yet confirmed can still be replaced by a conflicting one. The toy ledger above also shows only the principle, because a real network has no single machine that keeps the set.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Mining and Difficulty adjustment

items.head: Mining
items.body: Mining is the process by which new blocks are produced and new bitcoins are created. The chapter describes it as repeatedly performing a computational task that references a list of recent Bitcoin transactions, and it says that any participant in the network may operate as a miner, using their computing devices to help secure transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Difficulty adjustment
items.body: The difficulty adjustment is the rule that keeps the pace of the network constant.

At the end of every period of 2016 blocks, the nodes compare the time that the period actually took with the intended two weeks and scale the target accordingly: the new target is the old target multiplied by the actual timespan and divided by the intended timespan.

slides.notes:
Mining fulfils two purposes that a central bank would otherwise fulfil. It creates the currency, because the miner who finds a block is rewarded with brand new bitcoins and the fees paid by recent transactions, and it secures the record, because the work spent on a block makes the block costly to rewrite. The chapter says that every 10 minutes, on average, one miner can add security to past transactions, and that mining decentralizes the issuance and clearing functions of a central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The word mining suggests that coins are dug out of the ground one by one. What the miner actually finds is a valid block, and the new coins are a payment attached to it. Mining is also not a guaranteed income: because the search is a lottery, a single machine may work for a very long time without finding a block, which is the reason for pools. Finally, the share of the reward that comes from new coins falls with each halving, and the miners' revenue then depends increasingly on fees.

---

Without an adjustment, the pace of blocks would depend on the number of machines. If many new machines joined, blocks would arrive in seconds and the schedule of the supply would run ahead of its calendar; if many machines left, the network would slow to a crawl. The whitepaper gives the same reason: to compensate for increasing hardware speed and varying interest in running nodes over time, the difficulty is determined by a moving average targeting an average number of blocks per hour (Nakamoto, 2008).

The adjustment lags: the network reacts only after a period of 2016 blocks, so in the short run the pace can differ much from 10 minutes. It also does not control the price or the supply directly; it controls the pace. The figure of 10 minutes is a target and an average, and the time to the next block follows a random distribution, so that a block can come seconds or an hour after the previous one.

slides.title: Byzantine Generals' Problem
slides.sub: generals agreeing to attack by messenger

items.head: What it is
items.body: The Byzantine Generals' Problem is a classical problem in distributed computing. The chapter describes it briefly as the problem of trying to get multiple participants without a leader to agree on a course of action by exchanging information over an unreliable and potentially compromised network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The problem was stated in 1982 by Lamport, Shostak and Pease, who wrote that reliable computer systems must handle malfunctioning components that give conflicting information to different parts of the system (Lamport et al., 1982).

slides.notes:
The problem is the abstract form of the challenge that a money network faces. The participants are the computers, the course of action is the next block, and the traitors are dishonest participants who want to double-spend. The chapter calls Satoshi Nakamoto's invention a practical and novel solution to this problem and says that its use of proof of work to achieve consensus without a central trusted authority represents a breakthrough in distributed computing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The solution is probabilistic, not absolute. A node can never be mathematically certain that a block is final; the chance that it will be reversed falls with every block added after it, which is the reason for waiting for confirmations. And the guarantee depends on an assumption, namely that honest participants control the majority of the computing power; the story of the generals stays a useful reminder that this assumption is what the security rests on.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: History

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The History section tells where Bitcoin came from. The chapter describes the system as first described in 2008 with the publication of a paper under the alias Satoshi Nakamoto, as started in 2009 on a reference implementation, and as left in April 2011 to a group of volunteers when its inventor withdrew from the public (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The five concepts of the section run from the past to the present. Prior digital currencies and Hashcash describe what existed before. The whitepaper and its author describe the proposal.

slides.notes:
History explains why the design looks as it does. Bitcoin was not invented from nothing: it combined prior inventions such as digital signatures and Hashcash, and it answered the failure of earlier centralized digital currencies, which were targeted by governments and attacked by hackers. A student who knows the history can distinguish what was new in Bitcoin from what was inherited.

Concepts in this section: Whitepaper, Reference implementation, Satoshi Nakamoto, Hashcash, Digital currencies before Bitcoin.

slides.title: Whitepaper and Reference implementation

items.head: Whitepaper
items.body: The whitepaper is the paper in which Bitcoin was first described. The chapter says that Bitcoin was first described in 2008 with the publication of a paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The title already states the proposal: a system for electronic cash in which the parties deal with each other directly, as peers. The paper's argument proceeds in order.

items.head: Reference implementation
items.body: A reference implementation is a program that serves as the standard against which other programs are compared. For Bitcoin it is the software that implements the protocol and that includes a wallet, known as Bitcoin Core, which the chapter says is derived from the original implementation written by Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
The paper matters because it states the design in the author's own words, and because every later description of Bitcoin is an interpretation of it. Its abstract proposes a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash that would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution, and it proposes a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network (Nakamoto, 2008).

The whitepaper is not a specification. It leaves out details that the software had to settle, and the system has changed since 2008 in ways that the paper does not describe. A second observation concerns vocabulary: the saved text of the paper does not contain the word blockchain at all, and it speaks of a chain of blocks and of the longest proof-of-work chain (Nakamoto, 2008). The author's identity does not affect the text, which can be checked on its own merits.

---

Bitcoin has no written specification that is complete in itself, so the behaviour of the reference implementation has in practice defined what is valid. This is why other programs that speak the protocol are tested against it. The chapter compares the situation with the web: a Bitcoin wallet is the most common user interface of the system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol HTTP, and many brands exist for both (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reference implementation is a practical standard, and not a guarantee of correctness. The phrase means that the program is the one against which the behaviour of others is judged, not that it is the only program that could exist. A student should therefore distinguish the protocol, which the chapter describes as a peer-to-peer network, from Bitcoin Core, which is one program that speaks it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Satoshi Nakamoto

items.head: What it is
items.body: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin and created its original reference implementation. The glossary of the book adds that they devised the first blockchain database, that they were the first to solve the double-spending problem for digital currency, and that their real identity remains unknown (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter states that the whitepaper was written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto.

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The name appears in the title page of the whitepaper, in the copyright line of old source files, and in the name of the satoshi unit. The author of the paper gave an email address in the paper, satoshin@gmx.com, and the site bitcoin.org (Nakamoto, 2008), but nothing in the text identifies a person.

slides.notes:
The question of the author matters less for a technical course than it might seem, and the chapter explains why. Satoshi Nakamoto withdrew from the public in April 2011, leaving the responsibility of developing the code and network to a thriving group of volunteers, and neither Nakamoto nor anyone else exerts individual control over the Bitcoin system, which operates on fully transparent mathematical principles, open source code, and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A system without an owner does not need a known founder.

Two pitfalls are common. The first is to treat claims about the identity as facts; the book says the identity is unknown, and so does this text. The second is to confuse the author with the unit: Satoshi Nakamoto is a person or group, while the satoshi, the unit of one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, is only named after the author. A student should also avoid appeals to the authority of the author, since the rules of Bitcoin are those enforced by the software that participants run today.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Hashcash
slides.sub: a hash with leading zero bits

items.head: What it is
items.body: Hashcash is a proof-of-work system proposed by Adam Back. His paper states that Hashcash was originally proposed as a mechanism to throttle systematic abuse of un-metered internet resources such as email and anonymous remailers in May 1997, and that its cost-function computes a token which can be used as a proof-of-work (Back, 2002).

Back's paper defines the Hashcash cost-function as finding partial hash collisions on the all-zero bit string, and notes that the fastest algorithm for computing partial collisions is brute force; the client can safely choose its own random challenge, and anyone can efficiently verify a published token (Back, 2002).

slides.notes:
Hashcash showed that a cost in computation could replace a cost in money or an identity check. The paper reasons that if there is a cost associated with sending each email, this may be sufficient to limit the scale of email abuse perpetrated by spammers (Back, 2002). Back's paper requires that a cost-function should be efficiently verifiable but parameterisably expensive to compute (Back, 2002), and the same two properties are what Bitcoin needed: expensive to produce, cheap to check.

Hashcash on its own does not solve double-spending: it limits the rate at which tokens can be produced, and the paper itself says that the server needs to keep a double spending database of spent tokens, to detect and reject attempts to spend the same token again (Back, 2002). Bitcoin removes the server: the whitepaper adds a chain of blocks, in which each block includes the hash of the previous block, and a rule that the longest chain, the one with the most work, counts as correct (Nakamoto, 2008). A second caution is that the cost of the work depends on hardware, which is why Bitcoin adjusts its difficulty.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Digital currencies before Bitcoin

items.head: What it is
items.body: Digital currencies before Bitcoin were the early attempts, starting in the late 1980s, to use cryptography to build digital money. The chapter's sidebar says that when cryptography started becoming more broadly available and understood in the late 1980s, many researchers began trying to use it to build digital currencies, and that these early projects issued digital money, usually backed by a national currency or a precious metal such as gold (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The sidebar frames three questions that anyone accepting digital money must answer: whether the money is authentic and not counterfeit, whether it can only be spent once, and whether no one else can claim that it belongs to them and not to the holder (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
The failures of these projects define the problem that Bitcoin solved. The chapter reports that although the earlier currencies worked, they were centralized and, as a result, were easy to attack by governments and hackers; they used a central clearinghouse to settle all transactions at regular intervals, and in most cases they were targeted by worried governments and eventually litigated out of existence, while some failed in spectacular crashes when the parent company liquidated abruptly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The lesson of the sidebar is not that digital money is impossible without a network of equals, but that a central operator can be a single point of attack or of failure. The chapter's conclusion is that to be robust against intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, a decentralized digital currency was needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student should read that as a claim about design robustness, not as a statement of what is legal in any country.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Standards and openness

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Standards section collects the two social mechanisms through which Bitcoin is documented and developed: the numbered improvement proposals through which changes are discussed, and the open source licence under which the software is shared. Both appear in the chapter indirectly, in the references to the recovery code standard and to the open source software that runs the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The first concept of the section is the Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, the document in which a change or a convention is specified. The second one is open source software, the legal and practical form in which…

slides.notes:
A system without an owner needs a way to evolve. Proposals must be written down, discussed, and accepted or rejected in public, and the code must be available to anyone who wants to check or reuse it. These two practices are what allow a community of volunteers, rather than a company, to maintain a system that holds real value.

Concepts in this section: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP), Open source software, W3C standard.

slides.title: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP)

items.head: What it is
items.body: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a numbered document in which a member of the community proposes a change to Bitcoin or describes a convention that programs should follow.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The example takes numbers directly from BIP 39.

slides.notes:
BIPs give a decentralized project a public memory and a procedure. Every proposal has a number, an author, a status such as Deployed, and a type such as Specification, and it is available for anyone to read; the header of BIP 39 shows these fields (Palatinus et al., 2013). Because wallets of different authors can follow the same document, a user can move from one program to another, which is only possible when the convention is written down.

A BIP is a proposal and not a law. Its header records a status, and BIP 39 carries the status Deployed (Palatinus et al., 2013), which says that programs implement it; a proposal without that status gives no one an obligation. The appendix of the book lists which proposals Bitcoin Core implements and since which release, and the lesson is that a change takes effect only when the software that participants run contains it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Open source software and W3C standard

items.head: Open source software
items.body: Open source software is software whose source code is available to everyone and whose licence allows it to be used, studied, changed and redistributed. The Open Source Definition states that open source does not just mean access to the source code, and lists criteria that the distribution terms must meet, among them free redistribution, the inclusion of source code, and permission for modifications and derived works (Open Source Initiative, 2026).

items.head: W3C standard
items.body: The World Wide Web Consortium, abbreviated W3C, is an international public-interest non-profit organisation where member organisations, a full-time staff and the public work together to develop web standards (World Wide Web Consortium, 2026). It was founded by Tim Berners-Lee in 1994. A finished standard of the consortium is called a Recommendation.

A standard moves through drafts and review by the member organisations and by the public before it becomes a Recommendation, and the finished document is the one that implementers are expected to follow.

slides.notes:
Openness is part of why a system like Bitcoin can be trusted without a company behind it. The chapter says that the Bitcoin protocol stack is available as open source software and can be run on a wide range of computing devices, including laptops and smartphones, making the technology easily accessible, and that Bitcoin operates based on fully transparent mathematical principles, open source code, and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Open source does not mean that the code has been reviewed by everyone, and it does not mean that anyone can change the rules of the network. A change in the code reaches the network only if enough participants choose to run it. The chapter stresses that wallets vary in quality, performance, security, privacy and reliability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), so a student should not assume that every program that handles bitcoin is of equal quality merely because the protocol is open.

---

Open standards are what let software from different makers work together on the web, and W3C is where many of them are agreed. This chapter uses two of its Recommendations as a bridge to identity: the Decentralized Identifiers v1.0 of 19 July 2022 and the Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0 of 15 May 2025 (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022) (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025). Both express, in a standard form, the idea that control belongs to whoever holds the keys.

A Recommendation is a standard and not a law: it binds only those who choose to implement it, and its authority comes from the number of programs that do so rather than from any power to compel. A document that exists is therefore not evidence that the technology it describes is in wide use, and a student should say that a standard specifies a thing rather than that it establishes it. The Recommendations of this consortium should also be told apart from the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals of the earlier section, which are produced by a different community with its own numbering and its own process, even though both are public, numbered documents that specify how something is to be done.

slides.title: Wallet
slides.sub: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin.
slides.notes:
A wallet is where the abstract rules of the network meet a human being. It decides how much of the work of validation the user does himself, who holds the keys that control the money, and what happens when a phone is lost. The chapter says that wallets vary in quality, performance, security, privacy and reliability, and that choosing a wallet is highly subjective and depends on the use and the user's expertise, so that it would be pointless to recommend a specific brand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The three classifications are independent and combine freely. The chapter notes that many wallets fall into a few groups, the three most common being the desktop full node, the mobile lightweight wallet, and the web-based account with a third party, but that the lines between categories are sometimes blurry because software runs on multiple platforms and can interact with the network in different ways (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student should therefore describe a wallet along all three dimensions.

slides.title: Wallet platform

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The platform of a wallet is the kind of device and software environment on which it runs. The chapter's section on the types of Bitcoin wallets categorises wallets first by platform and lists the desktop wallet, the mobile wallet, the web wallet and the hardware signing device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The platform determines how convenient the wallet is, how exposed it is to attack, and how much of the user's data is revealed to others.
The four concepts of this section follow the order of the chapter. Each is described by what it runs on, what it protects, and what the user must trust.

slides.notes:
Every platform trades one benefit against another. A desktop wallet gives control and autonomy but runs on a general-purpose computer; a mobile wallet is convenient but often relies on remote servers; a web wallet is the easiest to start with and gives up the most control; a hardware device offers the strongest protection of keys and needs a second program to do the rest. Knowing the pattern lets a learner judge any new wallet, not only the ones named in the book.

Concepts in this section: Desktop wallet, Mobile wallet, Web wallet, Hardware signing device.

slides.title: Desktop wallet and Mobile wallet

items.head: Desktop wallet
items.body: A desktop wallet is a wallet program that runs on a personal computer. The chapter says that it was the first type of Bitcoin wallet created as a reference implementation, and that many users run desktop wallets for the features, autonomy and control they offer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The operating systems it runs on are general-use ones such as Windows and macOS.

The wallet runs as an ordinary application of the operating system. It stores its keys and its database on the computer's disk, and it connects to the network either as a full node or through another program.

items.head: Mobile wallet
items.body: A mobile wallet is a wallet application on a smartphone. The chapter calls it the most common type of Bitcoin wallet and says that it runs on smartphone operating systems such as Apple iOS and Android (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's first wallet in the chapter's story is of this type: she downloads one of Joe's recommendations and installs it on her phone.
To avoid downloading and storing large amounts of data, the chapter explains, most mobile wallets retrieve information from remote servers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
The desktop wallet matters because it is the platform on which a user can run a full node and thereby need to trust nobody else. The chapter groups the desktop full node among the most common arrangements and notes that in it you control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Features that smaller devices cannot offer are also found here, such as the use of the wallet together with a node that validates the entire history.

Autonomy and control come at a price in responsibility. A desktop wallet protects nothing if the computer carries malicious software, and a lost or damaged disk loses the keys unless a backup exists. A student should therefore treat the desktop wallet as a choice for users who accept those duties, and should not assume that a program on a personal computer is more secure than a service run by professionals.

---

The phone is the device that people carry and use for everything, so a wallet on it is the natural way to receive and spend small amounts. The chapter describes these wallets as often a great choice for new users, many being designed for simplicity and ease of use, while there are also fully featured mobile wallets for power users (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The convenience has a privacy cost. The chapter warns that retrieving information from remote servers reduces your privacy by disclosing to third parties information about your Bitcoin addresses and balances (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second consideration is that a phone can be lost, stolen or reset, which is why the chapter follows the creation of the wallet at once with the recovery code.

slides.title: Web wallet and Hardware signing device

items.head: Web wallet
items.body: A web wallet is a wallet that is accessed through a web browser and stores the user's wallet on a server owned by a third party. The chapter compares it to webmail, because it relies entirely on a third-party server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The user types into a page what a desktop or mobile user would do in an application.
The wallet's data lives on a server that the provider runs.

items.head: Hardware signing device
items.body: A hardware signing device is a small device that stores keys and signs transactions using special-purpose hardware and software built into the device. The chapter says that such devices usually connect to a desktop, mobile or web wallet by a cable, by a short-range wireless link, or by a camera that reads QR codes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The flow follows from the idea of the digital signature.

slides.notes:
Web wallets are easy to start with, which is why they are popular, and they show the central trade-off of the chapter in its clearest form: simplicity against control. The chapter notes that most web wallets take control of the Bitcoin keys from users in exchange for ease of use, and that it is inadvisable to store large amounts of bitcoin on third-party systems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Convenience and safety should not be confused. A page in a browser looks like any other page, and the user cannot easily see whether the keys are on his device or on the provider's server. The advice of the chapter is plain: do not keep large amounts on third-party systems, and remember that dependence on the server reveals information about the user even in the best case.

---

The purpose is to keep the private key away from the computer or phone that is most exposed to attack. By handling all Bitcoin-related operations on the specialised hardware, the chapter says, these wallets are less vulnerable to many types of attacks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A device that only signs, and never shows the key, reduces the damage that malicious software on the connected computer can do.

The name hardware wallet is misleading, and the chapter says so in its own way: the device does not hold bitcoin, nor does it see the network, and it needs a second wallet. Its protection is limited to the keys. A student should also remember that the device is used with a recovery code, since a lost device has to be replaceable, and that the privacy of the paired wallet remains the privacy of the user.

slides.title: Node type

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The node type of a wallet describes how much of the network's work the wallet does for itself. The chapter's section Full node versus Lightweight classifies wallets by their degree of autonomy and by how they interact with the Bitcoin network, and distinguishes the full node, the lightweight client and the third-party API client (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fourth concept of the section explains the words peer and client that the chapter uses to describe the arrangement.
The section orders the node types from the most autonomous to the least. The full node validates the entire history. The lightweight client keeps the wallet locally and validates partially.

slides.notes:
Autonomy decides whom the user has to trust. A program that validates everything itself trusts nobody, a program that checks only part of the data trusts its sources for the rest, and a program that asks a remote service trusts that service completely. The three degrees line up with three levels of resource use, from heavy to light.

Concepts in this section: Full node, Lightweight client, Third-party API client, Peer and client.

slides.title: Full node and Lightweight client

items.head: Full node
items.body: A full node is a program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions, every transaction by every user, ever. The chapter adds that, optionally, full nodes can also store previously validated transactions and serve data to other Bitcoin programs, either on the same computer or over the internet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A full node therefore does not take anyone's word for what has happened.
A full node starts by obtaining the blocks of the chain from other nodes and checks each one against the rules of the protocol; it keeps only those that pass.

items.head: Lightweight client
items.body: A lightweight client, also known as a simplified-payment-verification (SPV) client, connects to a full node or other remote server for receiving and sending Bitcoin transaction information, but stores the user wallet locally, partially validates the transactions it receives, and independently creates outgoing transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The client cannot check the transaction for itself; by linking it to a place in the chain, the whitepaper says, the client sees that a network node has accepted it, and blocks added after it further confirm that the network has accepted it (Nakamoto, 2008).

slides.notes:
The full node is the one that gives the user complete autonomy, which is the chapter's term for needing to trust no one else. The price is resources: the chapter estimates that a full node uses about the same computer resources as watching an hour-long streaming video for each day of Bitcoin transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The whitepaper had foreseen the arrangement, and notes that businesses that receive frequent payments will probably still want to run their own nodes for more independent security and quicker verification (Nakamoto, 2008).

A full node is not necessarily a miner and not necessarily a wallet; it validates, and these other roles are added separately. It also does not make a payment faster or the network larger by itself. Its value is for its operator and for the network as a whole, since the more independent nodes check the rules, the harder it is to change the rules by force. A last point is that running one needs patience: the first download of the whole history takes a long time.

---

Most users cannot or will not run a full node on a phone, and the lightweight client is the practical answer. It keeps the one thing that cannot be delegated, the keys, and delegates the heavy task of storing and checking the chain. The whitepaper describes the method: a user needs only a copy of the block headers of the longest proof-of-work chain and a short proof that links a transaction to the block in which it is time-stamped (Nakamoto, 2008).

A lightweight client reduces its dependence on any single server by connecting to several peers, but the chapter is clear about the limit: the security of a client ultimately relies on the integrity of its peers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student should therefore read lightweight as a statement about validation and not about control: the client still holds the keys and still creates its own transactions.

slides.title: Third-party API client and Peer and client

items.head: Third-party API client
items.body: A third-party API client is a wallet that interacts with Bitcoin through the interfaces of a third-party system, instead of connecting to the Bitcoin network directly. The chapter adds that the wallet may be stored by the user or by third-party servers, but that the client trusts the remote server to provide it with accurate information and to protect its privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The client sends requests to the remote service, such as the balance of an address or the data of a transaction, and receives answers that it displays.

items.head: Peer and client
items.body: Peer and client are the two roles in the Bitcoin network, in the chapter's words. Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer network, and the full nodes are the peers: each peer individually validates every confirmed transaction and can provide data to its user with complete authority.
A peer-to-peer network has no server at its centre: each node can ask for data and give data. A client such as a phone wallet connects to one or more peers and asks them what it needs.

slides.notes:
This type is the least autonomous of the three, and it is included so that a student can see the whole range. A program that reads everything from a remote service has no means of checking that service. If the service is wrong, hacked or dishonest, the client cannot know, and the service learns what the client asks.

The trust placed in the remote server is complete. The chapter says that the client trusts the remote server to provide accurate information and to protect its privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and these two trusts can fail independently. If the keys are also held by the third party, the arrangement becomes a custodial one, which the next branch of the chapter treats.

---

The distinction explains where trust lies. A peer trusts its own checking, whereas a client trusts its peers. A general definition from the vocabulary of the internet agrees: a client is a system entity that requests and uses a service provided by another, called a server (Shirey, 2007). In Bitcoin the roles are more symmetrical, because every peer is also a server of data to others.

A client is not worse than a peer in every way: it can be much cheaper to run, and it still holds its own keys. The point is that its safety depends on someone else's honesty. A student should not describe the network as if every user were a peer, because most users, running wallets on phones, are clients.

slides.title: Key control

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs. If you are the only one with control over the keys, you are in control of your bitcoins; if you do not have control, your bitcoins are managed by a third party who ultimately controls your funds on your behalf (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Two concepts divide the section. The noncustodial wallet is the arrangement in which the user alone controls the keys and bears the responsibility for backing them up.

slides.notes:
The question decides who really owns the money. In the traditional financial system a bank holds the account and the customer holds a claim against it, whereas in Bitcoin the holder of the key holds the money itself. The chapter condenses the lesson into the sentence Your keys, your coins. Not your keys, not your coins, which its author says he coined to emphasise this point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Concepts in this section: Noncustodial wallet, Custodial wallet.

slides.title: Noncustodial wallet and Custodial wallet

items.head: Noncustodial wallet
items.body: A noncustodial wallet is a wallet in which the user, and only the user, controls the keys. In the story of the chapter, the wallet that Alice has chosen is a noncustodial wallet, so Alice (and only Alice) will be in control of her keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word custodial refers to a custodian, a third party who holds something on behalf of its owner; the prefix non- means that there is none.
The wallet creates the private keys on the user's device, keeps them there, and signs transactions on request. No server needs to approve a payment, and none can block one.

items.head: Custodial wallet
items.body: A custodial wallet, or account with a custodian, is the opposite of the noncustodial wallet: a third party controls the keys. The chapter divides key management software into two important categories based on control, wallets, where you control the keys, and the funds and accounts with custodians, where some third party controls the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The custodian keeps the keys in its own systems and maintains an account for each customer in its own records. A payment between two customers of the same custodian may not touch the Bitcoin network at all.

slides.notes:
Control of the key is the only prerequisite to spending: possession of the key that can sign a transaction is, according to the chapter, the only thing required to spend bitcoin, which puts the control entirely in the hands of each user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same fact has a hard consequence, which the chapter states at once: Alice bears responsibility for backing the keys up, since losing the keys means she loses access to her bitcoins.

Freedom from a third party is also freedom from its protection. There is no password reset, no support desk that can restore access, and no insurer. A student who recommends a noncustodial wallet to a beginner should recommend the backup with it. The chapter also warns that the real danger is fraud, since malware that mimics a wallet can trick the user into giving the code away.

---

Custody is convenient, and for that reason it is common. The user does not have to look after a backup or fear the loss of a device. The chapter lists web-based accounts with third parties as one of the three common groups of wallets, and says explicitly that in it you do not control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The price is that the bitcoin is in effect a claim on the custodian.

The risk lies with the custodian: if it fails, is hacked, or refuses a withdrawal, the customer has only a claim against it. The first sentence of the chapter's slogan states the remedy, and the second one states the cost. A fair reading is neither that custody is always wrong nor that it is safe, but that the user should know which arrangement he is in and how much he is willing to trust.

slides.title: Backup

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong. It begins with the chapter's account of Alice's first start-up, when her noncustodial wallet produces a recovery code that can be used to restore it, and it goes on to the additional data that a recovery code does not contain, and to the payments that some technologies keep outside the public blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The recovery code is the central concept, and the section also covers wallet metadata, the labels and notes of the user.

slides.notes:
In a system without a helpdesk, the backup is the only insurance. The chapter explains that the control of the keys brings the responsibility for them, and that a user who loses the keys loses the money. The section therefore treats the recovery code, the wallet's other data, and the newer payment methods in turn, because each has its own way of being lost.

Concepts in this section: Recovery code, Wallet metadata.

slides.title: Recovery code

items.head: What it is
items.body: A recovery code is a short secret, created by the wallet, from which all of the wallet's keys can be rebuilt.

rows: len('nephew dog crane clever quantum crazy purse traffic repeat fruit old clutch'.split())

items.head: How it works
items.body: In the BIP 39 convention, the wallet first generates random bits called the initial entropy, between 128 and 256 bits.

slides.notes:
The code makes the backup practical. A wallet contains many keys, and each new address uses a new one, but a single short code can restore them all. The chapter explains that if something happens to Alice's wallet she can download a new copy of her wallet software and enter this recovery code to rebuild the wallet database of all the onchain transactions she has ever sent or received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other names reflect its role: seed phrase, because it provides the input, the seed, to the function that generates all of a wallet's keys.

The code is the key to the money, and whoever sees it can take the funds, so it must be kept offline and private. The chapter's warning is explicit: malware applications mimic the design of a wallet, insist that you enter your recovery code, and relay it to the developer so that they can steal your funds, which is the equivalent of phishing websites. Most wallets ask for the code only at the initial set-up and during recovery; if an application asks at any other time, the chapter advises consulting an expert (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also notes that writing the phrase down on paper tends to be more reliable than memory, and that the code alone does not restore data such as labels.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Wallet metadata
slides.sub: labels attached to addresses and transactions

items.head: What it is
items.body: Wallet metadata is the information that a user adds to a wallet about his own transactions, such as the labels that he associates with particular addresses or transactions. The chapter points out that recovering from the recovery code will not by itself restore any additional data Alice entered into her wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The data is stored in the wallet's database, and not in the blockchain.

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: Joe meets metadata when his wallet suggests that he enter a label for the transaction, and he enters Alice, so that weeks or months later he will remember why he sent 0.001 bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Many wallets provide an additional backup feature beyond recovery codes, so that this data can be saved separately.

slides.notes:
Metadata is less valuable than money, but it is valuable in its own way. The chapter compares the loss to a request to review an old bank or credit card statement in which the name of every entity you paid, or who paid you, has been blanked out (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For a business or a person who must account for payments, a history without labels can be nearly useless even though the money is safe.

A recovery code is therefore a backup of the keys and not of the whole wallet. The chapter adds a second reason to keep a full backup: for wallets that use offchain payments, a mechanism that depends on onchain data cannot guarantee recovery of all of a user's bitcoins, so it is important to make frequent backups of the wallet database (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Labels may also be sensitive, since they describe who the user pays.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Usage
slides.sub: The Usage branch follows the chapter's story of Alice and Joe: how Alice receives her first address, how she acquires her first bitcoin, and how Joe sends it.
slides.notes:
Usage is where a learner first sees the system work. The abstract rules of the earlier branches become a few taps on a phone: an address on a screen, a code scanned by a camera, a status that changes from unconfirmed to confirmed. A student who can follow the story step by step has the picture to which every later technical chapter adds detail.

The story is a simplification, and the chapter says it in one sentence: in the next chapter we will look at the underlying transaction and propagation technologies in more detail (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reader should not conclude that a payment is only a scan and a tap. The warnings that accompany each step, about lost keys, phishing, reuse of addresses and irreversible mistakes, are part of the lesson.

slides.title: Address

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The Address section explains the destination of a payment. An address is what a person shares so that others can send bitcoin to his wallet, and it is the first thing Alice's new wallet produces when she presses Receive. The chapter's tip adds that there are a variety of Bitcoin addresses and invoice formats, and that both may be shared with other users who can then send bitcoin directly to the wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The three concepts of the section move from the object to its use.

slides.notes:
An address is at once harmless and revealing, and the section exists to keep the two apart. It is harmless because knowing an address does not allow anybody to take money: the chapter states that, unlike a bank account number, nobody who learns one of your addresses can withdraw from your wallet, because you must initiate all spends (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is revealing because every payment made to it is visible on the public record for ever, so the way a person uses addresses decides how much of his financial life becomes visible to others. The habits that follow from this cost nothing, which is why the chapter states them as a rule rather than as advice.

Concepts in this section: Bitcoin address, Invoice, Address reuse and privacy, Privacy.

slides.title: Bitcoin address
slides.sub: an address shown as a QR code

items.head: What it is
items.body: A Bitcoin address is the string of characters that identifies where a payment is to be sent. The chapter explains that Alice's wallet randomly generated a private key, which will be used to derive Bitcoin addresses that direct to her wallet, and that her addresses are simply numbers that correspond to her private key and that she can use to control access to the funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The glossary adds that an address looks like a string of letters and numbers.

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The address is the part of the payment that the sender sees. In the story, Alice presses the Receive button and the wallet shows her first Bitcoin address as a QR code, which Joe scans instead of typing the quite long address by hand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
Addresses make it possible to pay someone without any prior arrangement. Because the addresses are generated independently by the wallet without reference to, or registration with, any service, there is no company that must be asked and no list that must be updated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Anyone can create as many as they need, and the chapter compares giving out an address with asking others to send an email to your email address.

An address is not an account number. The chapter stresses that, unlike a bank account number, nobody who learns one of your Bitcoin addresses can withdraw money from your wallet, because you must initiate all spends (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also not a name: an address says nothing about its owner until it is connected to an identity, and the following concepts of the section explain how that happens.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Invoice
slides.sub: a QR code with an address and an amount

items.head: What it is
items.body: An invoice is a request for payment that a wallet can understand. The chapter says that there is a variety of Bitcoin addresses and invoice formats, and that addresses and invoices can be shared with other Bitcoin users who can use them to send bitcoins directly to your wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
